problem: 'Since the days of the Henrys' assumes the reader knows this means the medieval/Tudor kings named Henry; a listener may hear it as a family name.
new_text: Old Mr. Rivers, she said, was a simple man, but a gentleman and from as ancient a family as you could find. Marsh End had belonged to the Rivers family for as long as it had been a house: and it was, she declared, over two hundred years old—though it looked just a small, humble place, nothing compared to Mr. Oliver's grand hall down in Morton Vale. But she could remember Bill Oliver's father as a common needlemaker; and the Rivers had been gentry since the days of the old King Henrys, as anyone could see by looking in the church registers at Morton. Still, she admitted, the old master was like other folk—nothing much out of the ordinary: passionate about shooting, farming, and such things. The mistress was different. She was a great reader and studied a great deal; and the children had taken after her. There was no one like them in these parts, nor had there ever been; they had loved learning, all three, almost from the time they could talk; and they had always been "their own sort." Mr. St. John, when he grew up, would go to university and become a clergyman; and the girls, as soon as they left school, would look for positions as governesses: for they had told her that their father had some years ago lost a great deal of money through a man he trusted going bankrupt; and as he was no longer rich enough to give them inheritances, they would have to provide for themselves. They had lived very little at home for a long while, and were only here now to stay a few weeks on account of their father's death; but they did so love Marsh End and Morton and all these moors and hills. They had been in London and many other great cities; but they always said there was no place like home; and they were so good with each other—never quarreled or argued. She did not know where you could find such a close family.

problem: 'Yes, and deems, and is bound to deem, himself honored' is tangled (verb split from its object by an interrupting clause, subject omitted); 'aspires only for' is also unidiomatic. Hard to follow aloud.
new_text: "You need not be in any hurry to hear," he said. "Let me be frank: I have nothing attractive or lucrative to suggest. Before I explain, please recall my clear warning that if I helped you, it would be as the blind helping the lame. I am poor; for I find that, when I have paid my father's debts, all the inheritance remaining to me will be this crumbling house, the row of damaged firs behind, and the patch of moorland soil with the yew trees and holly bushes in front. I am obscure: Rivers is an old name; but of the three sole descendants of the line, two earn a dependent's wages among strangers, and the third considers himself an exile from his native land—not only for life but in death. Yes, and he considers himself honored by this fate, as he is bound to, and longs only for the day when the cross of separation from earthly ties shall be laid on his shoulders, and when the Head of that Church Militant of whose humblest members he is one shall give the word: 'Rise, follow Me!'"

problem: 'He startled at the word' is an awkward intransitive use of 'startle' that reads like a typo; 'gave a start' is the plain equivalent.
new_text: He gave a start at the word "ambitious." He repeated, "No. What made you think of ambition? Who is ambitious? I know I am: but how did you find that out?"

problem: 'The slip between the cup and the lip' alludes to a proverb ('there's many a slip twixt cup and lip') most modern readers won't know; without it the phrase is opaque. Brief in-line gloss keeps the allusion.
new_text: At that moment a small event occurred that seemed decreed by fate specifically to confirm the truth of the saying that "misfortunes never come alone," and to add to their troubles the maddening one of a good thing slipping away just as it seemed within reach—the old proverb's slip between the cup and the lip. St. John passed the window reading a letter. He came in.

problem: 'Die' is St. John's pet name for Diana, used here for the first and only time in this batch, straight after the news that the uncle is dead. Read aloud or on the page it sounds like the verb 'die'. The modern spelling 'Di' keeps the nickname without the confusion.
new_text: "What then, Di?" he replied, maintaining a marble stillness of expression. "What then? Why—nothing. Read."

problem: Typo: stray space after the closing em dash.
new_text: What did St. John Rivers think of this earthly angel? I naturally asked myself that question as I saw him turn to her and look at her; and naturally I sought the answer in his expression. He had already withdrawn his eyes from the Peri—this fairy vision—and was staring at a humble tuft of daisies growing by the gate.

problem: Tense error: 'is stationed there since' should be 'has been stationed there since'.
new_text: "I shall come up and help you teach sometimes," she added. "It will be a nice change for me to visit you now and then; and I do like a change. Mr. Rivers, I have been so merry during my stay at S——. Last night, or rather this morning, I was dancing until two o'clock. The ——th regiment has been stationed there since the riots; and the officers are the most delightful men in the world: they put all our young knife-grinders and scissor merchants to shame."

problem: The narrator suddenly addresses 'Mediocrity' as a person; as written ('Mediocrity—no:') it reads like an unfinished noun phrase, and the following 'you would live in hell' has no clear addressee. Making the direct address explicit fixes it.
new_text: "I have come to see how you are spending your holiday," he said. "Not in gloomy thought, I hope? No, that is good: while you draw you will not feel lonely. You see, I still worry about you, though you have held up wonderfully so far. I have brought you a book for the evening," and he laid on the table a new publication—a poem: one of those genuine masterworks so often granted to the fortunate public of those days—the golden age of modern literature. Alas! the readers of our time are less blessed. But take heart! I will not stop to accuse or lament. I know poetry is not dead, nor genius lost; nor has Mammon—the god of money—gained power over either, to bind or destroy them: they will both assert their existence, their presence, their freedom and their strength again one day. Mighty angels, safe in heaven! They smile when base souls triumph and timid ones weep over their destruction. Poetry destroyed? Genius banished? No! Mediocrity, no: do not let envy suggest that thought to you. No; they not only survive but reign and redeem: and without their divine influence everywhere, you would live in hell—the hell of your own smallness.

problem: Dangling modifier: 'Won over to religion in my youth, she has cultivated...' grammatically makes 'she' (religion) the one won over. Listeners will stumble on who 'she' is.
new_text: "No. There is this difference between me and deist philosophers, who believe in God but not in revelation: I believe; and I believe the Gospel. You chose the wrong word. I am not a pagan but a Christian philosopher—a follower of the faith of Jesus. As His disciple I embrace His pure, merciful, generous teachings. I champion them: I am sworn to spread them. I was won over to religion in my youth, and she has cultivated my original qualities like this: from the tiny seed of natural affection, she has grown the towering tree of love for humanity. From the wild, stringy root of human integrity, she has raised a proper sense of divine justice. The ambition to win power and fame for my wretched self, she has transformed into the ambition to expand my Master's kingdom; to win victories for the banner of the cross. This is what religion has done for me; making the best use of the raw material; pruning and training nature. But she could not root out nature: nor will nature be rooted out until this mortal puts on immortality."

problem: Dangling modifier: 'replacing the paper, I saw him' says Jane replaced the paper, but St. John did.
new_text: "Nothing in the world," was the reply; and, as he replaced the paper, I saw him deftly tear a narrow strip from the margin. It vanished into his glove; and with one hasty nod and "good afternoon," he was gone.

problem: 'Unbend your forehead' is an odd literal phrase; modern readers will not readily get 'you stop frowning / your face relaxes'.
new_text: "You relax your brow at last," said Mr. Rivers. "I thought Medusa had looked at you and you were turning to stone. Perhaps now you will ask how much you are worth?"
